subtitle: A February 1971 committee report listing quick fixes to the early Host/Host protocol and the choices it left open.

tldr.problem: After the Urbana meeting, the Host/Host protocol needed a quick review to find changes that were immediately desirable or necessary.
tldr.mechanism: A nine-member committee issued eight specific recommendations, such as byte-counted messages and new RST and RRP commands, and listed alternatives it could not settle.
tldr.outcome: The committee would canvass the network community and reconvene at UCLA on 8 March 1971 before final recommendations. This report was updated by RFC 107.

today: RFC 102 is a 1971 committee report whose status is recorded as Unknown, and it was updated by RFC 107. Its recommendations were proposals pending the 8 March 1971 meeting.

sections.title: The Glitch Cleaning Committee
sections.content:
At the NWG meeting in Urbana on 17 to 19 February 1971, a committee was set up to look at the Host/Host protocol and decide which changes were immediately desirable or necessary. It is chaired by Steve Crocker and has eight other members, from BBN, UCSB, Illinois, Lincoln, MIT and IBM.

The committee reached consensus on some topics and only proposed alternatives on others. It would canvass the network community, reconvene at UCLA on 8 March 1971, and decide on final recommendations, after which Steve Crocker would write Document #2. This sequence is used in place of the change procedure outlined in RFC 53.
sections.eli5: A small group met to tidy up the rules. They write down what they agreed, ask everyone else, and meet again to make it final.

sections.title: Specific Recommendations
sections.content:
The report makes eight recommendations. The ECO and ERP commands should each be 8 bits long and ERR should be 96 bits long. Message Data Types and the Cease mechanism should be dropped. A new pair of one byte commands, RST (reset) and RRP (reset reply), should be added: RST purges NCP table entries that came from the sending Host, and RRP acknowledges it. The committee recommends against making connections full-duplex.

Messages should be an integral number of bytes, and each message should say its byte count (a 16-bit number after the leader) and byte size (the next 8-bit field). The marking convention should be abandoned and the padding ignored. For flow control, the bits in a message are the product of bytes and byte size, and the leader and other fixed fields are not counted.

Interrupt synchronization on console input is treated as a third-level protocol matter: use INS to mean a special network-wide code has been inserted into the input stream.
sections.eli5: They agreed to make some commands tiny, add a reset button, drop two features, and have every message say how many pieces it has and how big each piece is.

sections.title: Unresolved Alternatives
sections.content:
Three topics were left open. First, whether to limit the length of control messages: either no special limit (about 1000 bytes) or 120 bytes. Second, where the first data byte of a message begins: either after 72 bits of leader, byte count, byte size and spacing, or using the double physical transmission scheme in RFC 67, where a leader, byte count and byte size are sent first and the data follows as a second transmission.

Third, allocation: leave the ALL, GVB and RET commands unchanged, or make flow control track two quantities, messages and bits. In the second option the sending NCP decrements a message counter by 1 and a bit counter by the text length, may not let either go negative, and the message counter would be 16 bits long.
sections.eli5: On a few questions the team could not pick one answer, so they listed the choices for everyone to vote on.
